messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh is a 48-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as a private tutor, mostly for elementary school children. She came to therapy at her husband’s urging, though she is not sure anything can help. She is certain she has been permanently changed for the worse, and that it is only a matter of time before someone harms her again.

The event that shattered her happened twelve years ago, when she was still with her previous partner, a man she had been dating for two years. He had a temper, but she never expected what happened that night. A small argument over money escalated, and he shoved her into the kitchen wall. She hit the back of her head and slid to the floor. While she was down, he grabbed her by the hair and forced her face to the ground. In the corner of her vision she saw a large chef’s knife on the counter, and she was certain he would pick it up. He did not. He left her there, bleeding from a split lip, and she managed to crawl to her phone and call a friend. That was the last time she saw him.

The memory comes to her in disconnected pieces that do not fit together in time. She sees the knife as if it were a photograph, a still image she can bring up any time, but she cannot recall how she got from the wall to the floor, only the impact. When the memory surfaces, so does the same terror she felt at that moment: her chest tightens, her hands go cold, and she feels the absolute certainty that she is about to die. It is not a memory; it is a re-living.

In the years since, Linh has built a life of careful vigilance. She married a kind, quiet man named Tom, but she has never been able to trust that he, or anyone, is safe. She has come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, and that anyone could be dangerous. She is constantly scanning every environment she enters for signs of threat. In a tutoring center, she notices potential weapons everywhere: a pair of scissors on a desk, a heavy stapler, even a metal ruler. She does not consider this paranoid; she considers it realistic. Her body reacts before her mind has time to think. A door slamming shut makes her flinch and her heart race before she registers that it was only the wind. She cannot stop it.

She checks mirrors compulsively. In her car, she glances at the rearview mirror repeatedly to make sure no one is behind her. In public bathrooms, she checks the mirror to see if someone has entered behind her. At home, she positions herself so that she can see the front door from the kitchen, and she avoids sitting with her back to a room. She is hypervigilant toward people, especially men who remind her of her ex-partner: tall, broad-shouldered, quick to raise their voice. She has become an expert at reading a person’s build and body language from across a room.

Her work as a tutor has been heavily affected. She only accepts female students or boys under the age of ten, because older boys and men make her too anxious to concentrate. This limits her client base and reduces her income, but she cannot force herself to take a male teenager. She insists on meeting at a public library and always chooses a table with her back to a wall and a clear view of the entrance. During sessions, she finds herself looking at the child’s backpack, then checking the nearby tables for anything that could be used as a weapon. One afternoon a father showed up early to pick up his daughter, and when he entered the reading room without warning, Linh startled so badly she dropped her cup of tea and felt dizzy for ten minutes. The girl’s mother gave her a strange look.

Linh feels like a complete outsider now, even among people who have known her for years. She used to be talkative and warm; now she is guarded and withdrawn. Tom’s family invites her to gatherings, but she cannot relax. She watches from the corner of the room, monitoring who comes in and out, and she often leaves early. She has come to believe that she is fundamentally different from others, that the abuse broke something inside her that can never be repaired. She does not talk about it because she assumes no one would understand.

What finally brought her to therapy was a conversation with her husband after a particularly bad week. She had screamed at him for coming up behind her in the kitchen, and afterward she saw the hurt in his eyes. He said he could not live like this anymore. She agreed to come, but she is not hopeful. The part of her that still wants to believe she can feel safe is the same part that she learned to silence a long time ago. She is terrified that if she lets her guard down, she will be hurt again — and she is equally terrified of living the rest of her life this way.
